references.text: Abraham sits at the tent opening in the midday heat and sees three men (the Lord and two angels). This parallels how Lot sits at the gate of Sodom in the evening and receives the two angels.
The men (angels) turned and went toward Sodom, while Abraham stood before the Lord to plead for mercy for the city.
Lot settled in the cities of the Jordan Valley and pitched his tents all the way to Sodom, which explains why he was sitting at the city gate.
The angels who came to Lot in verse 1 urge him at dawn to take his family and leave the city before it is destroyed.
After Lot leaves Sodom, the Lord rains down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah as punishment for their sin.
It encourages hospitality toward strangers, for some have unknowingly entertained angels—mirroring Lot's welcome of the angels at the gate of Sodom.
Peter uses the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of God's judgment on ungodliness and how the righteous Lot was rescued.
The letter of Jude mentions Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of punishment for sexual immorality and unnatural desires.
Both illustrate the same profound gesture of submission and reverence toward a divine angel.
